To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) standardization is a dynamic process that is driven by the adoption decisions of individual agents; 2) the process of standardization depends on agents' attitudes to incompatibility; and 3) official regulation may be useful in some circumstances.
standardization outcomes are determined by the degree of aversion to in-compatibility and that official action can be effective if aversion is high.

(1) standardization outcomes depend critically on adopters' aversion to incompatability; (2) incompatibility aversion is a key factor that determines the effectiveness of regulation in standardization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conditions under which standardization fails or succeeds in the presence of network externalities and decentralized decision making.
how the evolution of norms can be influenced by public intervention.
the conditions under which standardization is a problem, and with the role of government regulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
standardization is a process that is likely to happen, but that it may be desirable to regulate it if the standardization process takes too long, or if the outcome is inferior.
, in decentralized economies, regulation can help in some cases, but not in others.
the role of official action in standardization is to provide a backstop for the emergence of sensible standards in the presence of incompatibility-averse individuals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
standardization is a complex phenomenon that depends on many factors and that it cannot be explained by a unique model.

the more individuals dislike incompatibility, the less likely they are to adopt the best standard, the more likely they are to be locked in, and the more likely they need regulation to achieve sensible standardization.
the role of the state in standardization is not clear-cut and depends on the attitudes of the individuals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of regulation, standardization outcomes depend not only on the characteristics of the technologies involved, but also on the characteristics of individuals.

, in order to understand the emergence of standards and norms, it is necessary to look beyond their economic value, and take into account the psychological costs that individuals experience when they have to cope with incompatibility.
the design of standardization policies must take into account the degree of tolerance to incompatibility in the society.
